elements.content: Grammar focus: Future Forms.

Ask three questions: is the future fixed by a schedule, agreed with someone, or decided as I speak? Is my prediction based on evidence I can see, or on opinion? Will the action be in progress, or complete, at the reference time? Each answer picks a different form, and mixing them changes what the listener understands about how firm the plan is.

present simple — timetable, programme, schedule: the train leaves at 07:40
present continuous — arrangement with a time and a person: we are meeting the board on Thursday
going to — intention or evidence-based prediction: it is going to rain
will — decision now, offer, promise: I will send it today
will be + -ing — activity in progress at a future time: at ten we will be presenting
will have + participle — completed before a future point: by June we will have finished
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'By next year the company ___ three new plants.'
2. Complete: 'We ___ the client at ten tomorrow, so the file must be ready.'
3. Which sentence predicts from visible evidence?
options: Look at the sky: it is going to rain.

elements.content: Read and listen: three examples in context.

Arrangement — I am seeing the minister on Tuesday. (Fixed in a diary.)
Prediction from evidence — Costs are going to rise. (Visible now.)
Decision made now — I will send it today. (Announced at the moment of speaking.)
Deadline — By Friday we will have sent the file. (Completed before a future point.)
What do you observe?

The form follows the evidence. Present simple for timetables and programmes. Present continuous for arrangements already made with other people. Going to for intentions and for predictions with present evidence. Will for decisions taken at the moment of speaking, offers and promises. Will be + -ing for an activity in progress at a future time, and will have + participle for what is complete before a future point.
1. Which form fits a train timetable?
2. What does 'I'll send it today' usually signal?
options: A decision taken at the moment of speaking.

elements.content: State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: I can design a flexible work policy.

Success criteria:
- I can choose a future form by evidence and commitment.
- I can use the present simple for schedules and the continuous for arrangements.
- I can use will have + participle for deadlines.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ We will meet the board on Thursday (will for an arrangement already made) → ✅ We are meeting the board on Thursday
❌ By June we will finish the audit (will + base for a completed action before a deadline) → ✅ By June we will have finished the audit
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

The hearing starts at nine and ends at noon.
We are signing the contract on Friday.
By the end of March we will have trained every team.
Adapt the same task to the group:

- Individual: five sentences with the structure, on the topic of the lesson.
- Pair: a ten-line dialogue where future forms carries the argument.
- Group: a six-minute debate, two sides, the structure required in every turn.
- Professional audience: transpose the structure into a memo.
- Academic audience: transpose it into a paragraph of analysis.
